summary: FNV (Fowler/Noll/Vo) is a fast non-cryptographic hash with good dispersion that is widely used. This informational document makes information about it and open-source code for the specified sizes conveniently available. It is not meant to resist attackers.

plainLanguage.summary: FNV is a quick way to turn data into a short number for filing and lookup. It is not for secrets.

questions: how fast is fnv compared to sha256
can fnv be used for passwords
subtitle: A fast, simple algorithm for spreading data into lookup tables and hash tables.

tldr.problem: Hashing functions are used everywhere—lookup tables, databases, caches, DNS, symbol tables—but most cryptographic hashes are slow. Fast non-cryptographic hashes are needed for high-performance applications that do not require cryptographic strength.
tldr.mechanism: FNV (Fowler/Noll/Vo) is a simple algorithm that XORs each byte of input with a running hash, then multiplies by a prime number chosen for good dispersion across the hash space.
tldr.outcome: FNV has been widely adopted for decades in systems ranging from NFS and filesystems to web search engines, anti-spam filters, and game servers, and is now documented as an Informational RFC with reference implementations.

today: RFC 9923 is an Informational RFC documenting FNV as it has been implemented and used since the 1990s. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the current reference for FNV specifications and implementations.

sections.title: What FNV Is and Why It Exists
sections.content:
FNV is an acronym for Fowler/Noll/Vo, the three people who designed this fast non-cryptographic hash algorithm. The purpose of this RFC is to document FNV and make reference code conveniently available, since FNV has been in use for three decades but was never formally standardized. It is widely used in systems where speed and a small code footprint matter more than cryptographic security: NFS file systems, game consoles, DNS servers, symbol tables in compilers, caches at scale, and many databases.

Hashing is the process of turning a piece of data into a short fingerprint (usually a number). A good hash function spreads data evenly across the possible hash values, so that two similar inputs (like two URLs differing by one character) produce unrelated hashes. FNV excels at this dispersion property, especially for nearly-identical strings. It is also extremely fast, with the algorithm requiring just a few CPU operations per byte of input – far faster than cryptographic hashes like SHA-256.
sections.plainLanguage: FNV is like a mail-sorting machine: you feed it text, and it spits out a number. It does so very quickly and spreads similar text to different numbers. But if you know how it works, you can compute what number it will give before running it.

sections.title: How FNV Works
sections.content:
The FNV-1a algorithm is simple: start with an offset_basis (a magic starting number chosen for the hash size). For each byte of input, XOR it into the hash, then multiply the result by the FNV Prime (another carefully chosen number). This is done modulo 2^HashSize to keep the result within the desired bit width.

The algorithm supports multiple output sizes: 32-bit, 64-bit, 128-bit, 256-bit, 512-bit, and 1024-bit hashes. Each size has a different Prime and offset_basis, chosen through a mathematical process to maximize dispersion. The FNV Prime for 32-bit hashes is 16,777,619; for 64-bit, it is 1,099,511,628,211. Smaller hashes can be derived from larger ones using XOR folding: hash a larger output, then XOR portions of it together to shrink it.
sections.plainLanguage: FNV is three steps repeated for each byte: XOR, multiply, and keep only the bottom N bits. Choose the magic starting number and the magic multiplier carefully, and you get a great spreading property.

sections.title: Uses and Limitations
sections.content:
FNV shines in non-cryptographic applications: hash tables in memory, file fingerprints, symbol tables, DNS servers, memcache implementations, and anti-spam filters all use or have used FNV. It can be used to generate flow IDs for network packets (like IPv6 flow labels) or to implement fast lookups in caches. Because XOR operations are simple and cheap, FNV can hash large amounts of data with low latency, and it can process multiple independent pieces of data in parallel by continuing from a previous hash result.

However, FNV has important limitations. It is not cryptographically secure. The low-order bits of the hash are simple XORs of the low-order bits of the input, making it easy to predict. An attacker can compute collisions offline and feed specially crafted inputs to cause denial-of-service by filling a hash table with collisions. FNV should never be used for passwords, MACs, digital signatures, or any security-critical application. The RFC explicitly recommends using cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 or SHAKE256 when facing an active adversary.
sections.plainLanguage: FNV is great for quick lookups and spreading data. But if someone can see your hash outputs and is trying to break your system, they can craft inputs that all hash to the same bucket. For secrets, use a real cryptographic hash.

sections.title: Constants and Variations
sections.content:
The FNV algorithm includes carefully selected prime numbers and starting values (offset_basis) for each supported hash size. The 32-bit offset_basis is 2,166,136,261 (0x811C9DC5), computed by FNV-hashing the ASCII string chongo <Landon Curt Noll> /\../\. This choice of starting point has the nice property that hashing an empty string returns exactly the offset_basis, making it observable if a system is vulnerable to collision attacks.

The RFC also covers practical variations: XOR folding to shrink hashes to non-standard sizes, hashing multiple values by chaining (computing FNV of one value, then using that result as the offset_basis for the next), and parallel hashing by dividing the input and hashing pieces independently then combining the results. Endianness is specified as little-endian for persistent storage and interoperability between systems.
sections.plainLanguage: FNV has magic numbers for each hash size, and the RFC lists them all. It also shows tricks for combining FNV results and for shrinking the output to odd sizes.

sections.title: Security Limitations and Collision Resistance
sections.content:
The RFC devotes significant space to security, emphasizing what FNV is not. An attacker with offline knowledge of the hash function can pre-compute collisions and submit them to degrade service. However, if the system uses a non-standard offset_basis (one the attacker does not know), collisions become much harder to construct. This is one defense: keep the offset_basis secret, or choose it randomly per system instance.

The high-level lesson is: FNV is fast and reliable for data structuring and lookup, but it is not a security tool. It does not resist deliberate collision attacks. Each layer of a system should use the appropriate tool: FNV for hash tables, SHA-256 for cryptographic commitments, and higher-level constructs like HMAC for message authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: FNV is not a lock – it is a label maker. If someone knows the recipe, they can forge labels to crash your system. Use a secret offset_basis to slow them down, but use real cryptography for anything security-critical.
